episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Indigenous Lands & Innovation
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Indigenous Lands & Innovation.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Who gets to leave, and who has to stay?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down South Cariboo Recreation Centre adds $10K in accessibility upgrades and MEET THE CANDIDATE: City council candidate Sheila Boehm, plus 10 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Who holds the authority to decide what Indigenous governments' financial records, cultural objects, and services are judged by, and whether sovereignty survives federal funding conditions and clawbacks? Topics include: The FSIN audit dispute, ISC clawback threats, and who controls eligibility rules, Data sovereignty, digital audit trails, and vendor lock-in for Indigenous governments, Repatriation of the Kawacatoose tipi cover and the role of digital cataloguing versus institutional decisions, Verification of residential school closure dates at Lebret, Gordon, and Muscowequan, Governance models for Indigenous child and family services, including Denisiqi Services Society and Tŝilhqot'in title.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Denisiqi Services Society

discussion.central_question: Who holds the authority to decide what Indigenous governments' financial records, cultural objects, and services are judged by, and whether sovereignty survives federal funding conditions and clawbacks?
discussion.riley_position: Indigenous nations should keep their own transparent audit trails and digital records, which preserve sovereignty and let them contest federal findings; sovereignty and federal funding can coexist if the terms are written down and understood.
riley_key_evidence: FSIN disputes ISC's audit decision over $12.4 million, with the legal action being the nation using its own jurisdiction to test the number
The Kawacatoose tipi cover, taken in 1926 and held at the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian, was returned to Kawacatoose First Nation
Denisiqi Services Society has run culturally grounded child and family services for Tŝilhqot'in and Ulkatcho communities for more than twenty years
discussion.casey_position: Records and courts do not resolve who ultimately controls the money and eligibility rules; clawbacks threaten current services, restitution requires institutional decisions rather than tools, and sovereignty claims remain untested until a court rules.
casey_key_evidence: ISC has threatened to claw back all current funding if FSIN does not repay the $12 million flagged in the audit, and the department issuing the audit is the one moving to collect
The Kawacatoose cover was returned only after a community meeting with Smithsonian representatives, and it took a century, while a scan is not a substitute for return

The Lebret residential school closure date of June 30, 1998 is solidly sourced, but the 1990s claim for Gordon and Muscowequan remains unverified, and testimony must be checked against records before being repeated as fact
discussion.resolution: The hosts did not reach agreement. Riley maintained that records and nation-held systems let a nation contest findings and that sovereignty can coexist with funding agreements; Casey stressed that the department writing the rules also collects the money, and that the sovereignty question remains open until tested in court. They agreed the key questions to carry forward are who holds the audit trail and who can change reporting terms after funds are released.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the actual status and substance of the FSIN–Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) forensic audit dispute, and does it hold up as a case of funding accountability versus Indigenous governance?

Findings: The Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (FSIN) received ISC's final forensic audit decision, rejected it, and launched legal action over roughly $12.4 million in spending that ISC deems ineligible under funding agreements. Regional outlets put the figure at "more than 12.3 million" in some reports, so the exact number varies by outlet. The FSIN says it denies wrongdoing and that it participated fully in the review. CTV reports ISC is moving to collect the money and has threatened to claw back all current funding if FSIN does not repay the $12M flagged in the audit. The Global News article's body text is mostly reader-comment material and does not explain the audit's findings, so the substance has to come from these other reports. Note that the FSIN's public position is framed around sovereignty, while the funding relationship it is contesting runs through the Indian Act-era contribution framework.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue that the audit shows the value of independent forensic review and that Indigenous governments should be building their own transparent financial systems and digital audit trails. Casey can counter that the dispute is less about bookkeeping than about who controls money meant for First Nations, and that a clawback threat on current funding puts pressure on the services the federation delivers. Use the sovereignty framing as a sharp point of tension: if FSIN claims sovereign status, does it accept federal audit authority, and can it be both? Keep the discussion on the documented facts (the dispute, the legal action, the threatened clawback) and avoid guessing at specific misspending.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What are the verified details of the Kawacatoose tipi cover repatriation, and how does it fit into the broader museum-repatriation story?

Findings: CBC reports the tipi cover belonged to sîpiskwêsîkan (also known as Dustyhorn) and was taken from Kawacatoose First Nation in 1926. It was held at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum for a century before returning to his descendants. Indiginews and CBC describe a community ceremony in which Chief Cory Dustyhorn, a descendant, first touched the painted cover. Indiginews says the cover was painted in the early 1920s. The return came after the community met with Smithsonian representatives in Washington, D.C.

Suggested angle: This is the most natural "innovation" thread in the set, but it is about cultural restoration, not technology. Riley can use it to ask whether digital cataloguing, 3D documentation, or virtual access could help other nations find and request their objects. Casey can push back that the central fact is a physical object held for a century without consent, and that digital access is no substitute for return. The best exchange is whether innovation here means new tools or simply the old work of restitution finally being done.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Are the residential school claims in the Eagle Feather News piece consistent with the historical record on when Saskatchewan's schools closed?

Findings: The Eagle Feather piece says Gordon and Muscowequan residential schools were operating through much of the 1990s. Records give mixed signals. The Lebret (Qu'Appelle) school closed on June 30, 1998, after 114 years, according to the Regina Leader-Post. The Lebret school is also listed on the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR) site as operating 1884–1998. For Muscowequan, CBC reports the Catholic church operated the school until the federal government took it over in 1969, and Wikipedia notes it was later converted to a student residence. This does not settle the 1990s claim for Muscowequan, and the Eagle Feather article should be treated as a survivor-testimony source rather than a verified timeline.

Suggested angle: Use this as a fact-checking moment in the episode. Riley can say the final-generation framing matters because it challenges the story that residential schools ended in the 1970s and 80s. Casey can stress that survivor testimony is powerful, but the dates need careful sourcing before they are repeated as fact. Make clear which school dates are confirmed (Lebret, 1998) and which are still unclear (Muscowequan, Gordon).

ELECTION RESEARCH — 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject.

**FINDINGS — Cariboo-Chilcotin**

Filed candidates: Kathryn Askew (BC NDP), Lorne Doerkson (Conservative), Douglas Gook (BC Green). Elections BC's candidate report lists all three (elections.bc.ca, candidate website report, Oct. 2026), and BC Ballot and Studio X News carry the same names.

- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).** 100 Mile Free Press (Oct. 1, 2026) reports she is a retired school teacher from Canim Lake, named as the NDP candidate. The BC NDP release names her as its Cariboo-Chilcotin candidate (bcndp.ca, undated in my read) and says she has 32 years in education, including leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union. The release also says that in 2025 she was the NDP candidate for Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford in the federal election. I did not find her vote share in that race. Stephen Taylor's 2025 results page reports Brad Vis (Conservative) won that riding with 56.7% and Jeff Howe (Liberal) placed second with 36.6% (stephentaylor.ca, 2025 results). No controversy involving Askew was found in the sources read.

- **Lorne Doerkson (Conservative).** Sourced background: MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, first elected as a B.C. Liberal, re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). BC Ballot gives the 2024 Conservative margin in the riding as 7,722 votes (bcballot.ca, 2026 candidate page). Carried forward from prior research: Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes shows him at 6,600 votes (51.25%) for the Liberals. The Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026) reports he took over as Conservative leader. Wikipedia describes him as interim leader since 2026.
  - *Controversy (campaign, 2026):* Vaughn Palmer's Vancouver Sun column (Oct. 7, 2026) says Doerkson told reporters he had made "no promises at all" on auto insurance, and Palmer argues he had made four. Palmer writes that Doerkson twice denied making commitments of any kind. This is the columnist's assessment, and the outlet's article was paywalled in my read. Doerkson's response is the denial reported in that column.
  - *Related party matter (not about Doerkson personally):* The Tyee (Oct. 8, 2026) reports Doerkson fired the party's Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after social media posts the BC NDP flagged as racist. CityNews (Oct. 14, 2026) reports a Conservative campaign director under fire over social posts will stay on, Doerkson says.
  - No other controversy involving Doerkson was established in the sources checked.

- **Douglas Gook (BC Green).** Elections BC's candidate report lists him for Cariboo-Chilcotin (2026). The Caledonia Courier (Oct. 2024) reports he had run unsuccessfully as a Green candidate in North Cariboo, now Prince George-Cariboo North, four times, including a 2017 Nechako Lakes bid where he took about nine per cent. My Cariboo Now calls his 2020 bid his fourth time running for the Greens in that riding. Carried forward from prior research: the Elections BC 2020 statement of votes shows him at 707 votes (6.38%) in Cariboo North. The two accounts don't reconcile the count of runs, and the show has not resolved it. CKPG Today (Sept. 13, 2024) announced him as the Green candidate for Nechako Lakes in 2024. His 2024 result in that riding was not established in the sources read. No controversy was established.

**FINDINGS — Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

Filed candidates: Denice Bardua (BC NDP), Sheldon Clare (Conservative), Randy Thompson (BC Green). The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports the list was confirmed by Elections BC after nominations closed Oct. 3. CKPG Today (Oct. 3, 2026) and the Prince George Citizen (candidates finalized) list the same three.

- **Denice Bardua (BC NDP).** CKPG Today (Sept. 24, 2024) reports she was announced as the NDP candidate for this riding in 2024. Her campaign site (denicebardua.bcndp.ca) says she has been a Quesnel resident since 1997 and works in education. BCPoliTracker reports she placed second in 2024 with 3,426 votes, or 17.0%, behind the Conservative candidate. Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) gives 17.03% for 2024. Her 2024 run is the only earlier run established in the sources read. No controversy was established.

- **Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent).** Sourced background: won the riding for the B.C. Conservatives in 2024 (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). Carried forward from prior research: Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports 11,430 votes, or 56.82%, in 2024. Times Colonist (Jan. 8, 2026, Canadian Press) reports he said he was running for the B.C. Conservative leadership. CFJC Today (Feb. 28, 2026) reports he suspended that bid, citing a leadership application issue where some signatures were not accepted. He said he "takes full responsibility."
  - *Election-finance penalty (finding):* Elections BC's enforcement notice (dated March 30, 2026) and its April 1, 2026 release (reported by CKPG Today, Apr. 1, 2026, and the Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Apr. 3, 2026) say he was fined $1,500 for accepting anonymous contributions for the 2024 election that exceeded the limit by about $4,000. Elections BC said the investigation found no deliberate attempt to circumvent the law. The Prince George Citizen reported the same penalty. I did not find his response to the penalty in the sources read.
  - *Allegation (Sept. 2026):* CKPG Today (Sept. 18, 2026) reports that in a party group chat about municipal elections, Clare wrote "There's a good number that need hanging," responding to a post by a Parksville mayoral candidate. Clare's statement says the remark was made in jest, was not meant as a threat, and he apologized to anyone who took offense (CKPG Today, Sept. 18, 2026; Prince George Citizen update). The Prince George Citizen headlined his apology as a formal apology. The BC NDP wrote on X that Doerkson "had one last chance to drop him. He didn't." That is the NDP's claim, and Doerkson's response to it was not found.
  - *Allegation (undated in snippet):* PressProgress reports residential-school postings attributed to Clare. The article says neither Clare nor the party responded to its requests for comment. The article's date and full text were not confirmed in my read, and the content appears to predate the 2026 campaign.

- **Randy Thompson (BC Green).** BC Greens' candidate page says he ran as the Green candidate in this riding in 2024 and previously served two years on the party's provincial council (bcgreens.ca). Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports he finished fourth in 2024 with just over four per cent. BCPoliTracker gives 866 votes, 4.3%. Prince George Daily News (Oct. 11, 2026) reports the Greens announced him as the candidate. No controversy was established.

The show has not yet established any earlier provincial election run for Kathryn Askew, Denice Bardua or Randy Thompson.
